sec:
Vote by mail or absentee

Can’t get to your polling place on Election Day? Here is how to vote by mail in Arizona, from the state’s own election office and its laws. Checked October 21, 2026.

Ask for your ballot by

Friday, October 23Passed

Your request must reach your county recorder by 5 p.m. on Friday, October 23, 2026 (the law says 5 p.m. on the 11th day before the election). If you are already on the Active Early Voting List, you do not need to ask again unless the ballot should go to a different address. (the law)

Send it back by

Tuesday, November 3Passed

Your ballot must be received by 7 p.m. on Tuesday, November 3, 2026. A postmark is not enough: a ballot that arrives after 7 p.m. on Election Day is not counted. The state's voter-education commission recommends mailing it no later than Tuesday, October 27, 2026 (7 days before), and dropping it off after that. (the law)

The last day to ask for a ballot by mail has passed. You can still vote in person, early or on Election Day, Tuesday, November 3.You can still vote in person on Election Day, Tuesday, November 3. Early voting in person runs through Friday, October 30, 2026. When and where to vote early.

Ask for a ballot online, on Arizona’s own site

At school away from home, in Arizona or in another state? What Arizona says about students is under Show more.

Who can vote by mail

Any registered voter may vote by early ballot. You can ask for a ballot for one election, or join the Active Early Voting List so a ballot is mailed to you for every election you can vote in. (the law)

How to ask for a ballot

  • Online. Ask for a one-time ballot by mail on the state's Arizona.Vote request page. To get one every election, join the Active Early Voting List through ServiceArizona's voter registration form. Open it (official page)
  • Phone or e-mail. Contact your county recorder by phone or e-mail, or through the recorder's website. State law lets you ask by voice or in writing; you give your name, address, date of birth and state or country of birth (or other facts that match your voter record). (the law)
  • By mail. Send a signed written request to your county recorder with the same information. (the law)

How to send it back

  • By mail. Mail it back in the envelope provided; postage is prepaid. It must arrive by 7 p.m. on Election Day, so mail it by October 27. (official page)
  • Drop box. Any secured ballot drop box in your county, by 7 p.m. on Election Day. (official page)
  • In person. Any voting location or polling place in your county, or your county recorder's office, by 7 p.m. on Election Day. You do not have to wait in the voting line to drop it off. Starting in 2026, the law also lets you bring it to a polling place in your county and choose to show valid ID there. (the law)

What the envelope needs

Sign the affidavit on the back of the return envelope; a ballot without your signature is not counted. No ID is needed to vote by mail: the county compares your signature with your voter record. If the signature does not match or is missing, the county tries to reach you, and you have until the fifth business day after the election (Tuesday, November 10, 2026) to fix it. No witness is needed. Only you, a family member, someone in your household, or your caregiver may return your ballot. (the law)

Track your ballot

Track your ballot on Arizona’s own site (official page)

Vote early in person instead

Wednesday, October 7, 2026 to Friday, October 30, 2026.

In-person early voting starts 27 days before the election and runs through the Friday before Election Day (until 7 p.m. under state law). Bring ID. Locations include the county recorder's office; hours vary. If an emergency comes up after 7 p.m. that Friday, you can ask to vote in the way your county sets up until 5 p.m. on Monday, November 2. (the law)

Students

At school in Arizona, away from home

Register with the address you consider your home; it decides your district and what is on your ballot. If you are living away from home for school, tell your county recorder your new mailing address so the ballot is mailed to you. You can vote only in the county where you are registered; for example, a student registered in Maricopa County going to school in Coconino County gets the ballot from Maricopa County, or goes back home to vote, and must return the ballot to the right county by 7 p.m. on Election Day. (official page)

At school in another state, with Arizona as home

The state says you will need to decide whether you are still an Arizona resident (you intend to return) or a resident of the new state; you may be registered in only one place. If you stay registered in Arizona, contact your county recorder before each election and ask for the ballot to be mailed to your out-of-state address. Return it so it reaches your county by 7 p.m. on Election Day. If you register in the other state, cancel your Arizona registration. The state notes that residency can affect tuition and scholarships and suggests asking your school. (official page)

Military and overseas

Military voters, their family members, and overseas citizens can register and ask for a ballot with the Federal Post Card Application, and use the Federal Write-In Absentee Ballot as a backup. Ballots are mailed to them 45 days before the election. They can return a ballot by fax or through the Secretary of State's secure upload system; it must be received by 7 p.m. on Election Day. (official page)

Arizona in the Federal Voting Assistance Program’s guide

Good to know

  • In Arizona a postmark does not count: the ballot must be in the county's hands by 7 p.m. on Election Day.
  • Ballots are not forwarded by the post office. If you are away, ask your county recorder to mail the ballot to where you are.
  • Maricopa County voters can also sign up for text and e-mail alerts about their ballot with the County Recorder; Pima and Navajo counties have their own trackers.
  • The Secretary of State also runs a ballot tracker with alerts, linked from the Commission's Election & Ballot Tracking page (not opened here).
  • State law says a person does not gain or lose a residence just by being a student somewhere (A.R.S. 16-593).
  • A one-time request can ask for the ballot to go to a temporary address (A.R.S. 16-542); the Active Early Voting List form asks for a mailing address in your county of residence (A.R.S. 16-544).

How this was checked

  • The Secretary of State's own site (azsos.gov) and the Arizona.Vote portal refused this check's requests, so the facts come from Arizona law and from the Citizens Clean Elections Commission, the state agency for voter education. The request and tracking links were taken from the Commission's pages and were not opened here.
